summary: Flame in Freefall is an interactive web app that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into clear fire safety insights. NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database holds decades of space combustion experiments, but the results are hard to find, compare, and understand. The app summarizes 24 PSI combustion investigations with full provenance (1,984 observed test rows), ranks them against an explicit, adjustable fire safety rubric, and supports extractive search that quotes source records alongside clearly labeled AI-written annotations. A live AI layer (large language model) interprets a selected investigation record, ranks investigations against a chosen criterion, and synthesizes findings across investigations; every AI output is labeled as interpretation and traceable to the NASA record fields or curated index passages behind it. An interactive simulator shows the canonical microgravity flame - an isolated fuel droplet burning as a spherical diffusion flame - using the classical d-squared law; the flame size follows a theory model and is labeled as an estimate, not a measurement. Model residuals are reported against 257 graded FLEX (PSI-69) experiment runs. Data extracts (JSON/CSV) support further modeling. It is an educational and research tool; it cannot judge whether a spacecraft is safe. All sources are credited.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Explore: 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations (19 flight experiments, 5 ground/analysis studies) with objectives, hardware, publications, DOIs, and per-file statistics, from the PSI repository (snapshot 2026-11-14). Rank: investigations scored against an explicit, adjustable fire safety rubric. Ask: deterministic extractive search over the frozen PSI corpus - no external AI service; answers quote source records and show AI-written annotations clearly labeled as AI interpretation. Simulate: an isolated fuel droplet burning in microgravity, the case studied in NASA's FLEX experiments. Check: a bounded nearest-record lookup with regime separation - conditions outside the recorded regime are shown as unknown, not estimated. AI interpretation: a live large language model interprets a selected investigation record, ranks investigations against a chosen fire safety criterion, and synthesizes findings across investigations; each AI output is labeled as interpretation and traceable to the NASA record fields or curated index passages (team annotations) behind it. Results are mapped to spacecraft fire prevention, detection, and suppression, with Earth applications noted.

HOW IT WORKS

A physics forward model integrates the classical quasi-steady d-squared law (droplet diameter squared shrinks linearly in time). Gas mixture transport uses standard mixing rules with two fuel-vapor conductivity candidates (an extrapolated NIST vapor fit and the Chung 1988 corresponding-states correlation); the comparison between the two candidates is exploratory. Model residuals are reported per fuel, diluent, and variant, with the run count n shown for each cell. Flame standoff (flame diameter / droplet diameter) follows classical theory (Matalon lecture notes, Princeton CEFRC); during the modeled burn, the drawn flame-to-droplet ratio follows the computed ratio. Separately, burns can be replayed using the measured burning-rate constant K from NASA data. The comparison cohort is from PSI-69 (FLEX) only: 274 recorded runs, 258 with measured K, 257 graded.

AI interpretation layer: for an investigate request, the app sends the full original NASA record fields plus the team's annotations for the selected investigation to a hosted large language model over a free, usage-capped API; for rank and synthesis requests it sends curated passages from the team's index. Outputs must follow a structured format citing the supplied material and pass traceability and structure checks before display; an output that fails or is unavailable is shown as unavailable, never silently replaced. Team annotations are labeled as team annotations wherever cited. Physics computations and extractive search remain deterministic and separate from the AI layer.

HONEST LIMITS

The standoff ratio is a theory estimate that overpredicts measured values. Agreement with historical data varies widely and is presented as a comparison, not a validation. Flame texture, flicker, and pointer lean are visual effects. AI-written annotations in the app are interpretive aids, not NASA findings. The app cannot judge spacecraft fire safety. AI interpretations are generated by a language model from the cited material and pass format and traceability checks, but they can still be wrong; they are reading aids, not NASA findings, and not a validated fire-safety recommendation.

WHY IT MATTERS

Fire safety in crewed spacecraft depends on understanding flammability without buoyancy, and planned Moon and Mars habitats are expected to use higher oxygen concentrations, which raise flammability. NASA's PSI database holds the relevant experiment record, but it is hard to find, compare, and interpret. This app makes that record explorable for students, researchers, and engineers.

TOOLS AND AI USE

Hosted web app built with React + TypeScript and procedural WebGL visuals. Live AI interpretation runs on a hosted large language model over a free, usage-capped API; physics computations and search are deterministic, kept separate from the AI layer. Development disclosure: code, data preparation, documentation, and visual design were developed with SI (AI) assistance; outputs were checked against the cited sources. Four unmodified NASA photographs are used (GRC-2016-C-05051, iss040e021546, iss040e072900, iss040e086481).

NASA DATA USED

PSI data repository (24 combustion investigations, harvested 2026-11-14); FLEX experimental table (PSI-69); FLEX detailed-results report (NTRS 20150023456); Flame in Freefall challenge background.
